title: AutoTag and AutoSnap: Standardized, semi-automatic capture of regions of interest from whole slide images
author: Marien, Andries, et al.

steps.title: Stain tissue and scan whole slide
steps.instruction: Stain tumor sections for CD31 using the NCL‑CD31‑1A10 antibody (Leica Biosystems, Diegem, Belgium) on a Ventana Benchmark® XT platform, then scan each slide on a Pannoramic SCAN (3DHISTECH) scanner.

substeps.instruction: Use a 20× Plan Apo objective (0.80 NA) and a Hitachi HV‑F22CL 3CCD progressive‑scan color camera.
Set image resolution to 0.23 µm/pixel, JPEG quality factor to 80, and interpolated focus distance to 15.
Enable stitching and configure a specific scan profile for each slide; fill holes in the scan area to ensure correct tissue detection.
After scanning, examine the whole‑slide image to confirm image quality and that the entire tissue section is captured.

steps.title: Create point annotations with AutoTag
steps.instruction: Open the scanned slide in Pannoramic Viewer (build 1.15.4.43061, 3DHISTECH) and run the AutoHotkey script AutoTag in the background to automate point‑annotation naming.

substeps.instruction: In the viewer, select the point‑annotation tool and click each desired location (ROI) on the image.
AutoTag monitors the screen, creates a point annotation at each click, and assigns a sequential number starting from 1.
Continue until all required ROIs are annotated.

steps.title: Determine minimum ROI count via bootstrapping
steps.instruction: Calculate the smallest number of ROIs needed for reliable microvessel‑density measurement by bootstrapping.

substeps.instruction: Select 25 ROIs on a CD31‑stained colorectal carcinoma slide (i = 1…25).
For each ROI compute microvessel density QA = Σ Ni / Σ Vi,ref, where Ni is the vessel count and Vi,ref the number of grid points hitting tissue.
Resample the 25 ROIs with replacement 1000 times and calculate QA for each resample.
Plot the coefficient of variation (CV) of QA versus the number of ROIs and fit a trend line f(x) = a x⁻ᵇ.
Compute the derivative f′(x) = ‑a b x⁻ᵇ⁻¹; the minimum ROI number is reached when the derivative falls below 0.50 %.
Applying this analysis to 19 colorectal, 22 renal cell, 21 glioblastoma, and 21 ovarian carcinoma cases indicated that 10 ROIs are sufficient.

steps.title: Set magnification and export annotation list
steps.instruction: After all point annotations are created, let AutoTag prompt for the imaging magnification, choose 20× (sufficient for microvessel identification), and generate a summary file.

substeps.instruction: AutoTag writes a .txt file with three columns: sample name, number of annotations, and chosen magnification.

steps.title: Generate snapshot images with AutoSnap
steps.instruction: Run the second AutoHotkey script AutoSnap, which reads the .txt file and automatically creates centered snapshot images for each annotation.

substeps.instruction: AutoSnap saves each image with a standardized filename at a predefined folder location.
Include sleep/pause functions to accommodate software or network lag; typical runtime is ~66 s per image (vs. 19 s for manual creation).
The process can run unattended (e.g., overnight) because no user input is required.

steps.title: Prepare digital grids in Photoshop
steps.instruction: Create two transparent digital grids in Adobe Photoshop: a 5 × 5 field grid and a 9 × 9 field grid, each covering 2500 µm², intended for 40× and 20× magnifications respectively.

steps.title: Apply grids to images via Bridge batch
steps.instruction: Use Adobe Bridge to batch‑process the AutoSnap images with a self‑written Photoshop action that overlays the appropriate grid layer and saves the result as a new image.
